Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM . SGLang Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s: python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 4 \ --attention-backend trtllm_mha \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell): python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 8 \ --attention-backend fa3 \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 Inference Providers Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon. import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "https://router.huggingface.co/v1" , api_key=os.environ[ "HF_TOKEN" ], ) completion = client.chat.completions.create( model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto" , messages=[{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is the capital of France?" }], ) print (completion.choices[ 0 ].message) Inference Endpoints We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4 , or install with the hf cli like so: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam What we tested We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809 Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088 * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. Post-training Beam You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT with TRL The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes. After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself. Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR . GRPO with Miles Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty. Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute. Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch. Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty. The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn. Train with LoRA You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading. python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 Build with Beam: Demos If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . To inspire you, here are a few things we built. Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application! At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out. We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text. Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account. Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery. We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements. You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace . If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions . Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents? We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. items.content: Back to Articles TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 30 +24 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron. Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx . New backend, native interface in HF libraries To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron . This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so. TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile . For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron. Transformers Inference Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices. The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations. import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401 from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B" MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024 PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512 dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) world_size = dist.get_world_size() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.bfloat16, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size), device_mesh=DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range (world_size))), ). eval () tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) if tokenizer.pad_token is None : tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token tokenizer.padding_side = "left" inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "The future of AI is" }], add_generation_prompt= True , padding= True , tokenizer_kwargs={ "pad_to_multiple_of" : PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE}, return_tensors= "pt" , ) generation_config = GenerationConfig( max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , use_cache= True , pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, cache_implementation= "static" , max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN, prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE, compile_config=CompileConfig(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= False , dynamic= False ), ) with torch.no_grad(): output_ids = model.generate( inputs[ "input_ids" ], attention_mask=inputs[ "attention_mask" ], generation_config=generation_config, ) if dist.get_rank() == 0 : prompt_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] print (tokenizer.decode(output_ids[ 0 , prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens= True )) Training Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings. Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer . If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar. import os import torch from datasets import load_dataset from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser def main ( script_args, training_args, model_args ): # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660) torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False training_args.model_init_kwargs = { "revision" : model_args.model_revision, "trust_remote_code" : training_args.trust_remote_code, "attn_implementation" : model_args.attn_implementation, "dtype" : model_args.dtype, "device_map" : None , } if int (os.environ.get( "WORLD_SIZE" , "1" )) > 1 : # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded training_args.model_init_kwargs[ "distributed_config" ] = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ.get( "TP_SIZE" , "1" )), fsdp_size= int (os.environ.get( "FSDP_SIZE" , "1" )), ) # Prepare dataset train_dataset = load_dataset( script_args.dataset_name, name=script_args.dataset_config, split=script_args.dataset_train_split, ) # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset. train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns([ "messages" ]) # Training trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model_args.model_name_or_path, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir) trainer.end() if __name__ == "__main__" : parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig)) script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config() main(script_args, training_args, model_args) Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs , SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained , and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config. Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium: Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure. Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 . The command below launches training with torchrun , which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node . The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups. TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \ --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \ --dataset_train_split train_sft \ --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max_length 2048 \ --packing true \ --packing_strategy wrapped \ --learning_rate 2e-5 \ --warmup_steps 0.03 \ --num_train_epochs 1 \ --logging_steps 2 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --save_only_model true \ --torch_compile true We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance. Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware. Diffusers Inference Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP: import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig # Distributed devices initialization dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) # TP dev = torch.neuron.current_device() mesh = DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range ( 8 ))) # TP=8 # Pipeline initialization model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1" transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( model, subfolder= "transformer" , torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP ) pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( model, transformer=transformer, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe.vae.to(dev) pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) # Image generation emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt= "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting" , device= "cpu" ) # text encoder stays on CPU image = pipe( prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev), prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None , height= 1024 , width= 1024 , num_inference_steps= 40 , generator=torch.Generator( "cpu" ).manual_seed( 0 ), # same noise on every rank ).images[ 0 ] if dist.get_rank() == 0 : image.save( "out.png" ) You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py . More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . Kernels Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub. You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium! items.raw_text: Back to Articles TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 30 +24 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron. Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx . New backend, native interface in HF libraries To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron . This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so. TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile . For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron. Transformers Inference Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices. The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations. import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401 from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B" MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024 PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512 dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) world_size = dist.get_world_size() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.bfloat16, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size), device_mesh=DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range (world_size))), ). eval () tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) if tokenizer.pad_token is None : tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token tokenizer.padding_side = "left" inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "The future of AI is" }], add_generation_prompt= True , padding= True , tokenizer_kwargs={ "pad_to_multiple_of" : PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE}, return_tensors= "pt" , ) generation_config = GenerationConfig( max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , use_cache= True , pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, cache_implementation= "static" , max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN, prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE, compile_config=CompileConfig(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= False , dynamic= False ), ) with torch.no_grad(): output_ids = model.generate( inputs[ "input_ids" ], attention_mask=inputs[ "attention_mask" ], generation_config=generation_config, ) if dist.get_rank() == 0 : prompt_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] print (tokenizer.decode(output_ids[ 0 , prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens= True )) Training Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings. Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer . If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar. import os import torch from datasets import load_dataset from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser def main ( script_args, training_args, model_args ): # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660) torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False training_args.model_init_kwargs = { "revision" : model_args.model_revision, "trust_remote_code" : training_args.trust_remote_code, "attn_implementation" : model_args.attn_implementation, "dtype" : model_args.dtype, "device_map" : None , } if int (os.environ.get( "WORLD_SIZE" , "1" )) > 1 : # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded training_args.model_init_kwargs[ "distributed_config" ] = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ.get( "TP_SIZE" , "1" )), fsdp_size= int (os.environ.get( "FSDP_SIZE" , "1" )), ) # Prepare dataset train_dataset = load_dataset( script_args.dataset_name, name=script_args.dataset_config, split=script_args.dataset_train_split, ) # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset. train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns([ "messages" ]) # Training trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model_args.model_name_or_path, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir) trainer.end() if __name__ == "__main__" : parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig)) script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config() main(script_args, training_args, model_args) Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs , SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained , and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config. Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium: Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure. Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 . The command below launches training with torchrun , which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node . The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups. TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \ --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \ --dataset_train_split train_sft \ --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max_length 2048 \ --packing true \ --packing_strategy wrapped \ --learning_rate 2e-5 \ --warmup_steps 0.03 \ --num_train_epochs 1 \ --logging_steps 2 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --save_only_model true \ --torch_compile true We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance. Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware. Diffusers Inference Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . items.content: Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. items.content: Back to Articles NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required Enterprise + Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 23 +17 Joshua Przybylko jprzybylko Follow nvidia Valter Hudovernik valterh-nv Follow nvidia Federico Lopez flopeznv Follow nvidia Akihiro Nitta akihironitta-nv Follow nvidia Ramona Bendias RBendiasN Follow nvidia Ardrian Wong aw777 Follow nvidia Jure Leskovec profjure Follow nvidia Matthias Fey rusty1s Follow nvidia TL;DR NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers historical examples as context examples and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models and kumo-engine libraries, or as an NVIDIA NIM. items.content: Back to Articles Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 14 +8 Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub . We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps. Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not. Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post , we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row. Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function. + So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing. Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it. We call this offline policy-relative difficulty . We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run. What happened after training We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt. Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool. Metric Base RL fine-tuned Change Observed 20/20 38 (7.50%) → 107 (21.10%) +69 tasks pass@1 (successful attempts) 5,242 (51.70%) → 6,163 (60.78%) +9.08 pt pass@20 (tasks solved at least once) 453 (89.35%) → 446 (87.97%) −7 tasks Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff. What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20. Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19. Contents What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds Results: the dependability column moved Where the gains landed What dependability costs The training loop Offline policy-relative difficulty What earns a reward Run the training stack Where this goes next In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack . What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct. In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts . Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency. And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241 , on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability. If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires. The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark. Results: the dependability column moved After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training. Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most. The training loop Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench. Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run. Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat). Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py . For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps. Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures. That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool. Offline policy-relative difficulty Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer: No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation. ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim. Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] . If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] . In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another. ++ A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user. The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool? We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy. So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts: uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \ thinkingbox-eval \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --dataset " $THINKINGBOX_DATA " \ --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \ --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \ --repeat 20 \ --coverage-profile full \ --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \ --message-timeout 1800 The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards. If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records: Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and

ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not. Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post , we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Prepare the training data Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts: uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \ thinkingbox-eval \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --dataset " $THINKINGBOX_DATA " \ --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \ --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \ --repeat 20 \ --coverage-profile full \ --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \ --message-timeout 1800 The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards. items.content: Back to Articles Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 16 +10 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up .
